posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
Technically and practically impossible
the only way to get a perfect resize is to limit yourself to full multiples, 200%, 300%, 400% and so on.
Any resize value between those full values will either result in blur or result in distortions depending on the formula used for the resizing.
I don't have time now to explain the basics for you - but I already have done so a dozen times in other posts about zoom and resizing, so you might want to look for them.

@Andar

Forget about plugins - try opening the smaller image in an image editor and resizing it to the size of the larger one. Notice that whatever you do, some distortion is inevitable.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
AquaEcho said:
What if it's vector art? Does it still get distorted?
Click to expand...
yes and no
vectors don't get distorted, but you can't display vectors on any monitor display.
at some time in the process the vectors get turned into pixel becaused all displays work with pixels only.
and as soon as something is in pixels, any resize will distord it.
The advantage 3D graphics (vector-based graphics) have is that with modern 3D cards the conversion to pixel is the very last step, after resizing to fit the monitor.
with 2D graphics, the pixel is the basic unit and everything starts out as pixels.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
There are 2D and 3D vector images. Some Engines, such as Unity, can handle 2D vector images; basically the image is drawn with math and the computer recalculates those points as the resolution increases/decreases, drawing the necessary pixels between the points.
As Mac said, though, RM uses purely rasterized images; the pixels have already been set. So when scaling by non-integer values, the engine is going to have to guess at what pixels should be what color.
*integer scaling means scaling by a whole number. 1, 2, 3, etc. As opposed to 1.5, 2.6, etc.
When using a bi-cubic scaling seen in bg's Extra Large Harold
(to go , please)
, the overall image seems to be softened.
The nearest neighbor algorithm (what Pixel Perfect plugins do) does a better job at keeping the image crisp, but the result is that non-integer scaling needs to make assumptions about where to put pixels and the result is...well, you discovered it. Distortion.
The reason the image goes soft when going full screen is because you are scaling the image up to fit the resolution of your screen.
A game at 1080p can scale perfectly up to a 4k screen, but any screen (for example 2k/1440p) between 1080p and 4k will not integer scale.
A game at 720p can scale perfectly up to a 2k screen, but won't scale perfectly to 1080p or 4k.
Anyways, Mac and Andar said it best in less words, but hopefully you learned something here.
